title: Closed class hierarchies
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

The `closed` modifier on a class (C# 15) means it can be derived from only inside its own assembly. Because the compiler then knows every direct descendant, a `switch` that handles each one is exhaustive without a discard arm, just as with unions.

A closed class is implicitly abstract and cannot also be `sealed`, `static` or explicitly `abstract`. It suits state machines and domain alternatives that share data or behaviour through the base class, for example `closed record GateState` with `Open` and `Closed` records.
Closure is not transitive: a non-closed descendant can still be extended in other assemblies. Mark intermediate classes `closed` too if you want exhaustiveness further down the hierarchy.

Choose between the two C# 15 tools by shape: a union when the alternatives are unrelated existing types, a closed hierarchy when the alternatives are your own types that share a base. Check that adding a new descendant is meant to break incomplete switches, because that is exactly what it will do.

challenge: Model an expression tree with closed record Expr and descendants Num(double), Add(Expr, Expr), Mul(Expr, Expr). Write Eval with an exhaustive switch and evaluate (2 + 3) * 4.
question: Why does a switch over a closed class need no discard arm when it handles every direct descendant?
correct: Only the declaring assembly can add descendants, so the compiler knows them all
wrong: Closed classes are sealed, so only the base type can appear
The runtime throws for unknown types anyway
reasoning: closed fixes the set of direct descendants at compile time, enabling exhaustiveness checks.
